description: We are Ares Mars; Like the pioneers who've launched America to the moon, we are driven by logic, collaboration, and most importantly, passion; Driven to kickstart advancement. Whether it be learning unfamiliar program languages, or configuring the "perfect pitch", we have the capabilities of Scientists and Engineers that will display our creativity and future impact on society.
summary:
Our project is a 3D Mars navigation system that helps future astronauts explore the surface safely. We used real NASA satellite images and elevation data to build the terrain around Jezero Crater. You can look around, pick a place to go, and the site finds a route for you. It doesn’t just pick the shortest path. It also checks how steep the ground is, so the route is safer.

We also put a lot of science info in one place, like NASA Mars Trek, geology maps, Perseverance rover photos, and Mars weather data. We also started working on a small wearable device with an ESP32 so astronauts can check directions while they walk.

Right now, all this data is spread out across different websites. Our project puts it together so astronauts can see what’s around them, avoid hazards, and plan better trips.

Our goal is to show that data NASA already has can be turned into something useful for future Mars missions.
details:
Our project is an interactive 3D Mars navigation system built around Jezero Crater. We wanted to help future astronauts move around the Martian surface safely, and a flat 2D map didn’t seem like the best way to do that. So we combined real NASA data into one 3D environment: HiRISE satellite imagery, elevation models, geologic maps, and photos from the Perseverance rover.

To build it, we processed the NASA elevation and imagery data with QGIS and Python so it could run in a browser, then used Three.js, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Vite to turn it into terrain you can explore. Users pick a destination and the site finds a route with an A* pathfinding algorithm. Instead of only looking at distance, our algorithm also considers elevation changes and slope, so it can choose a safer route even if it isn’t the shortest.

We also added science information to make the map more useful. NASA Mars Trek gives geographic context, USGS geologic maps help explain the terrain, and Curiosity rover weather data from Gale Crater is included as a reference. Since that weather was measured in Gale Crater and not Jezero, we made sure to label it as reference data and not as actual conditions at Jezero.

We also started exploring a wearable navigation device using an ESP32 microcontroller, environmental sensors, and a touchscreen, so astronauts could check their route without carrying a full computer. Next, we want to add ESA’s HRSC terrain and global color mosaic so users can zoom out from Jezero to a much larger view of Mars.

Our goal was to show that existing planetary data can be turned into a practical tool for future exploration. If astronauts can spot hazards earlier, avoid unnecessary travel, and spend more time on science, that makes a mission better. We want exploring Mars to feel more intuitive and easier to understand.
